summary: BBN answers a recurring question: can a host computer be attached to a Terminal IMP's multi-line controller ports over serial lines? They now say yes, but warn that host connections to IMPs were assumed error-free, whereas phone lines are not, so the setup may not work as hoped.

plainLanguage.summary: Can you plug a big computer into the little terminal box? The answer was once no, now it is maybe, but the wire may make mistakes, so be careful.

subtitle: The limits of connecting hosts through terminal interfaces

tldr.problem: People ask whether a host computer can connect to the ARPANET through a Terminal IMP's Multi-Line Controller, as an alternative to a direct host-to-IMP interface.
tldr.mechanism: BBN explains that while it is technically possible, the approach has significant drawbacks: the connection lacks error control, bandwidth is limited, and the terminal-oriented command language does not support the full range of host-to-host operations.
tldr.outcome: BBN permits the arrangement but cautions that it is unlikely to work well in practice, and invites feedback from anyone who tries it.

facts.label: Standard host-IMP cable length
facts.value: Up to 30 feet (or up to 2000 feet with Distant Host option)

today: RFC 241 is an informational document and has not been obsoleted. It records BBN's engineering position on a specific connectivity question in the early ARPANET. The limitations it describes influenced architectural decisions in later network designs.

sections.title: The Question and the Constraint
sections.content:
Host computers normally connect to an IMP (Interface Message Processor) via a direct, error-free connection over short, shielded cables. The ARPANET relies on the assumption that host-to-IMP connections are reliable.

Some people ask whether a host can instead connect through a Terminal IMP's Multi-Line Controller (MLC), which is designed to handle connections over phone lines from remote terminals. BBN has historically said no, but this RFC changes that to a conditional yes.
sections.plainLanguage: The network was designed so big computers connect directly with no mistakes. Some people want to use the phone-line system instead, which was not designed for that.

sections.title: The Practical Problems
sections.content:
The Terminal IMP's MLC lacks error control. It was designed for human operators at terminals, where occasional character errors can be fixed or retried. A host-to-host connection will see the same errors but cannot tolerate them the same way.

Phone lines introduce errors that a direct cable does not, and the present Terminal IMP hardware and software provide no error recovery. Strong error control, like the system used for IMP-to-IMP links, would require major changes to both the Terminal IMP and the remote host.

Additionally, the Terminal IMP has limited bandwidth to share among its many connections, and the command language is designed for interactive terminals, not for the multiple simultaneous connections a host typically needs.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone lines make mistakes, the little box was not built to fix them, and even if you connect, the box will not let you do many of the things a host needs.

sections.title: BBN's Position
sections.content: BBN says it has no objection to the arrangement and is even interested in hearing about real experience if someone tries it. However, people should understand the constraints and limitations up front. If the connection works well for a particular use case, that would be valuable feedback. If it does not, the technical reasons will be clear.
sections.plainLanguage: Feel free to try it, but do not be surprised if it does not work well. If it does, please tell us.
